CIND820 Capstone Project¶

01 - Data Understanding¶

Dataset: Global Carbon Project - Global Carbon Budget 2022 (GCB2022v27)

Purpose of this notebook:
This notebook performs the initial structural and quality assessment of the Global Carbon Project fossil CO₂ emissions dataset. The analysis examines the dataset dimensions, variables, observation period, country/entity coverage, duplicates, missing values, and other characteristics before preprocessing and modelling.

Entity and ISO Code Findings¶

The dataset contains 232 entity series. Six entities do not have ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes: French Equatorial Africa, French West Africa, Kuwaiti Oil Fires, Leeward Islands, Pacific Islands (Palau), and Ryukyu Islands.

These six entities account for 1,632 rows, which is consistent with 6 entities observed across 272 years. The dataset also contains non-country aggregate entities such as Global (WLD) and International Transport (XIT).

No entities have been removed at this stage. These observations are documented because the final modelling population will need to distinguish standard countries from historical, aggregate, and special-purpose entities.

1.4 Data Completeness Across Historical Periods¶

The dataset extends from 1750 to 2021. Since detailed emissions-source data may be less available in earlier years, this section examines whether data completeness improves in more recent historical periods.

In [20]:
core_cols = [
    "Total",
    "Coal",
    "Oil",
    "Gas",
    "Cement",
    "Flaring",
    "Per Capita"
]

period_results = []

for start_year in [1750, 1800, 1850, 1900, 1950, 1960, 1980, 1990, 2000]:
    subset = df[df["Year"] >= start_year]

    complete_rows = subset[core_cols].notna().all(axis=1).sum()
    total_rows = len(subset)
    complete_percent = (complete_rows / total_rows) * 100

    period_results.append({
        "Start Year": start_year,
        "Total Rows": total_rows,
        "Complete Rows": complete_rows,
        "Complete Percent": round(complete_percent, 1)
    })

period_summary = pd.DataFrame(period_results)

Initial Descriptive Findings¶

The numerical emissions variables contain no negative values. However, many observations contain zero emissions, particularly in the Total, Gas, Cement, and Flaring variables. Because the dataset extends back to 1750, the occurrence of zeros will be investigated by historical period before any preprocessing decision is made.

The distributions are highly skewed. For Total emissions, the median is 0 MtCO₂ while the maximum exceeds 37,000 MtCO₂. Examination of the ten largest Total values showed that all belong to the Global aggregate rather than individual countries. Therefore, aggregate entities such as Global should be considered separately when defining the country-level modelling population.

Zero-Value and Extreme Per-Capita Findings¶

Zero Total-emissions observations are heavily concentrated in the earlier historical period. When the complete dataset from 1750 onward is considered, 65.5% of available Total-emissions observations are zero. This falls to 10.2% from 1950 onward, 8.3% from 1960 onward, and 4.8% from 2000 onward. This suggests that the high frequency of zero observations is strongly related to the long historical coverage of the dataset.

The largest Per Capita values were concentrated in Sint Maarten (Dutch part) during the 1950s. These observations have relatively small Total emissions but extremely high per-capita values, indicating that small-population entities can create extreme per-capita observations. These values should therefore be investigated rather than automatically treated as errors.

period_assessment = []

    "Total",

]

for start_year in [1900, 1950, 1960, 1980, 1990, 2000]:

    subset = df[df["Year"] >= start_year]

    total_rows = len(subset)

    complete_rows = subset[core_cols].notna().all(axis=1).sum()
    complete_percent = (complete_rows / total_rows) * 100

    valid_total = subset["Total"].dropna()
    zero_percent = ((valid_total == 0).sum() / len(valid_total)) * 100

    period_assessment.append({
        "Start Year": start_year,
        "Rows": total_rows,
        "Core Complete %": round(complete_percent, 1),
        "Zero Total %": round(zero_percent, 1)
    })

Entity Scope Findings¶

The dataset contains 232 entity series. Eight entities were flagged for special review because they either lack standard ISO codes or represent aggregate or special-purpose series such as Global and International Transport.

These entities have not been removed during the data-understanding stage. They are being documented separately so that the final country-level modelling population can be defined using clear and reproducible inclusion and exclusion criteria.

1.9 Relationship Between Total and Source-Specific Emissions¶

The Total fossil CO₂ variable is closely related to source-specific emissions such as Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other. This section examines those relationships to understand the structure of the target variable and to identify potential target leakage risks before feature engineering and modelling.

In [39]:

Coal 0.971885 1.000000 0.909819 0.884516 0.923924 0.860256 0.980136
Oil 0.977693 0.909819 1.000000 0.961722 0.853986 0.943509 0.906095
Gas 0.961426 0.884516 0.961722 1.000000 0.884847 0.911846 0.884148
Cement 0.921383 0.923924 0.853986 0.884847 1.000000 0.804896 0.962628
Flaring 0.921414 0.860256 0.943509 0.911846 0.804896 1.000000 0.878138
Other 0.956970 0.980136 0.906095 0.884148 0.962628 0.878138 1.000000

Correlation Findings¶

The source-specific emissions variables show strong positive correlations with Total emissions. Oil, Coal, Gas, Other, Cement, and Flaring all have correlations above approximately 0.92 with Total in the available observations.

These strong relationships are expected because the source-specific variables contribute to overall fossil CO₂ emissions. As a result, using same-year source values to predict same-year Total emissions would create a risk of target leakage and would not represent a valid forecasting task.

For future modelling, source-specific variables will therefore be considered as historical or lagged predictors when forecasting the following year's Total emissions.

The source variables are also strongly correlated with one another, which may introduce multicollinearity for linear regression models and will require further assessment during feature engineering.

Correlation Heatmap¶

A heatmap is used to visually summarize the strength of the relationships among Total and source-specific fossil CO₂ emissions variables. Darker or stronger cells indicate stronger correlations. This helps identify variables that move together and highlights potential multicollinearity and target-leakage concerns.

In [40]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

heatmap = ax.imshow(correlation_matrix, aspect="auto")

ax.set_xticks(range(len(correlation_matrix.columns)))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(correlation_matrix.index)))

ax.set_xticklabels(correlation_matrix.columns, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticklabels(correlation_matrix.index)

for i in range(len(correlation_matrix.index)):
    for j in range(len(correlation_matrix.columns)):
        ax.text(
            j,
            i,
            f"{correlation_matrix.iloc[i, j]:.2f}",
            ha="center",
            va="center"
        )

ax.set_title("Correlation Heatmap of Emissions Variables")

fig.colorbar(heatmap, ax=ax, label="Correlation")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Heatmap Interpretation¶

The heatmap confirms strong positive relationships between Total fossil CO₂ emissions and the source-specific emissions variables. Oil, Coal, Gas, Other, Cement, and Flaring all show correlations above approximately 0.92 with Total.

These strong relationships are expected because the source-specific variables contribute to overall fossil CO₂ emissions. Therefore, same-year source variables should not be used to predict same-year Total emissions because this would introduce target leakage.

The source variables are also strongly correlated with one another, which suggests potential multicollinearity for linear regression models. This will be considered during feature engineering and model interpretation.

1.10 Emissions Trends Over Time¶

This section examines how fossil CO₂ emissions changed over time. Trend analysis helps identify long-term growth patterns, structural changes, and unusual periods before modelling. Because the dataset contains a Global aggregate series, it is useful for understanding the overall historical direction of fossil CO₂ emissions.

Global Trend Interpretation¶

Global fossil CO₂ emissions remain relatively low during the earlier historical period and increase substantially over time, with much stronger growth during the twentieth century and especially after the mid-1900s.

This indicates that the emissions series has a strong long-term trend and that the statistical behaviour of the early historical period differs from the modern period. This supports the earlier finding that the full 1750–2021 range may not be equally suitable for predictive modelling.

The trend will therefore be considered when selecting the final modelling period and designing a time-aware forecasting strategy.

To compare country-level emissions behaviour, Total fossil CO₂ emissions are plotted for Canada, the United States, China, and India. These countries were selected to provide examples of different national emissions scales and historical trajectories.

Selected Country Trend Interpretation¶

The selected countries show substantially different historical fossil CO₂ emissions trajectories. China and India display strong growth in more recent decades, while Canada and the United States follow different long-term patterns.

These differences demonstrate country-level heterogeneity in both emissions scale and historical behaviour. This is important for modelling because a single cross-country forecasting model must account for countries with different growth rates, emissions levels, and temporal patterns.

The result supports the literature finding that country-specific behaviour should be considered when evaluating model performance.

1.12 Distribution of Total Emissions¶

This section examines the distribution of Total fossil CO₂ emissions across countries in the latest year. The purpose is to determine whether the target variable is approximately balanced or strongly skewed by a small number of high-emitting countries.

In [49]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

plt.hist(
    latest_snapshot["Total"],
    bins=30
)

plt.title("Distribution of Total Fossil CO₂ Emissions in 2021")
plt.xlabel("Total Fossil CO₂ Emissions (MtCO₂)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Countries")

plt.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Distribution Interpretation¶

The 2021 Total fossil CO₂ emissions distribution is strongly right-skewed. Most countries have relatively low Total emissions, while a small number of high-emitting countries produce a long right tail.

These high values represent genuine differences in national emissions scale rather than automatically indicating data errors. The skewed distribution may influence regression modelling and evaluation metrics, particularly metrics such as RMSE that give greater weight to large prediction errors.

The effect of this skewness will therefore be considered during feature engineering, model evaluation, and interpretation rather than removing high-emitting countries solely because their values are large.

In [50]:
total_mean = latest_snapshot["Total"].mean()
total_median = latest_snapshot["Total"].median()
total_skewness = latest_snapshot["Total"].skew()

print("Mean Total emissions:", round(total_mean, 2))
print("Median Total emissions:", round(total_median, 2))
print("Skewness:", round(total_skewness, 2))

Mean Total emissions: 161.17
Median Total emissions: 8.54
Skewness: 11.02

Log-Transformed View of Total Emissions¶

Because Total emissions are strongly right-skewed, a logarithmic transformation is examined to better visualize differences among lower- and medium-emitting countries. The transformation is used here for exploratory purposes and does not yet represent a final modelling decision.

In [51]:
import numpy as np

log_total = np.log1p(latest_snapshot["Total"])

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

plt.hist(
    log_total,
    bins=30
)

plt.title("Log-Transformed Distribution of Total Fossil CO₂ Emissions in 2021")
plt.xlabel("log(1 + Total Fossil CO₂ Emissions)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Countries")

plt.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
In [52]:
print(
    "Skewness after log transformation:",
    round(log_total.skew(), 2)
)

Skewness after log transformation: 0.64

Log-Transformation Interpretation¶

The raw 2021 Total emissions distribution is highly right-skewed, with a skewness of approximately 11.02. After applying a log(1 + Total) transformation, skewness decreases substantially to approximately 0.64.

The transformed distribution provides a more balanced view of differences across countries and reduces the dominance of extremely large emitters in the visualization.

This result suggests that a logarithmic transformation may be useful for some modelling approaches, particularly linear regression. However, no final transformation decision is made at this stage. Raw and transformed representations will be evaluated during feature engineering and model development.

1.13 Total and Per-Capita Emissions¶

Total emissions and per-capita emissions measure different aspects of national fossil CO₂ emissions. This section examines their relationship in the latest available year to determine whether countries with high total emissions also necessarily have high emissions per person.

Total and Per-Capita Relationship¶

The correlation between Total and Per Capita fossil CO₂ emissions in 2021 is approximately 0.14, indicating a weak positive linear relationship.

This suggests that countries with high Total emissions do not necessarily have high emissions per person. Total emissions are influenced by the overall scale of a country's emissions, while Per Capita emissions represent emissions relative to population.

Therefore, Total and Per Capita provide different information about national emissions patterns. Per Capita may provide additional historical information for forecasting, but it will be used only as a lagged predictor to avoid target leakage.

Per-Capita Ranking Interpretation¶

The 2021 Per Capita emissions ranking differs substantially from the Total-emissions ranking. Countries/entities such as Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Trinidad and Tobago, and Brunei Darussalam have high emissions per person despite having much lower Total emissions than the largest national emitters.

This supports the earlier finding that Total and Per Capita emissions measure different aspects of fossil CO₂ emissions. Total emissions reflect the overall national scale of emissions, while Per Capita emissions reflect emissions relative to population.

The ranking also highlights an important scope issue: some ISO-coded observations, such as New Caledonia, are territories rather than sovereign countries. Therefore, the final modelling population will require a more rigorous country/entity inclusion rule before model development.

Ranking Overlap Interpretation¶

Only one entity, Saudi Arabia, appears in both the top 10 Total-emissions and top 10 Per Capita-emissions rankings for 2021.

This reinforces the finding that Total and Per Capita emissions capture different characteristics of national emissions. High overall emissions do not necessarily imply high emissions per person, and vice versa.

The Global aggregate is used specifically for this descriptive analysis. It remains excluded from country-level comparisons and the planned country-level forecasting population.

Global Source Composition Findings¶

For the Global 2021 observation, the sum of Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other emissions exactly matches Total fossil CO₂ emissions.

Coal is the largest source, contributing approximately 40.35% of Total emissions, followed by Oil at 31.89% and Gas at 21.34%. Cement, Flaring, and Other sources contribute much smaller shares.

This confirms that source-specific emissions are components of the Total variable. Therefore, using same-year source variables to predict same-year Total emissions would introduce target leakage. In the forecasting stage, source-specific variables will instead be considered as historical or lagged predictors.

1.15 Verification of Total Against Source Components¶

This section checks whether Total fossil CO₂ emissions are equal to the sum of Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other emissions when all source-specific values are available.

Only complete observations are used for this verification. Missing source values are not treated as zero.

)

    component_check["Total"] - component_check["Source Sum"]
)

component_check["Absolute Difference"] = (
    component_check["Difference"].abs()
)

Source-Component Verification Findings¶

Among the 1,619 observations with complete values for Total, Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other, the sum of the source-specific components matches Total emissions within 0.01 MtCO₂ for 100% of observations.

The maximum absolute difference is approximately 0.000002 MtCO₂, which is negligible and reflects numerical rounding rather than a meaningful discrepancy.

This provides strong evidence that, when all source components are available, Total emissions are constructed from the sum of Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other emissions. Therefore, using same-year source components to predict same-year Total would introduce direct target leakage.

For the forecasting task, source-specific emissions will instead be considered as historical or lagged predictors for forecasting the following year's Total emissions.

import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px

# Create the 2021 mapping dataset
map_2021 = df[
    (df["Year"] == latest_year) &
    (~df["Country"].isin(special_entity_review["Country"]))
][
    [
        "Country",
        "ISO 3166-1 alpha-3",
        "Total",
        "Per Capita"
    ]
].dropna(
    subset=["ISO 3166-1 alpha-3", "Total"]
).copy()

# Log-transform Total only for the map colour scale
map_2021["Log Total"] = np.log1p(
    map_2021["Total"]
)

print("Observations available for mapping:", len(map_2021))

# Create interactive world map
fig = px.choropleth(
    map_2021,
    locations="ISO 3166-1 alpha-3",
    locationmode="ISO-3",
    color="Log Total",
    hover_name="Country",
    hover_data={
        "Total": ":.2f",
        "Per Capita": ":.2f",
        "Log Total": False,
        "ISO 3166-1 alpha-3": False
    },
    title="Geographic Distribution of Total Fossil CO₂ Emissions in 2021"
)

fig.update_layout(
    coloraxis_colorbar_title="log(1 + Total)",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0)
)

fig.show(renderer="browser")

Observations available for mapping: 224

Geographic Distribution Interpretation¶

The 2021 world map shows substantial geographic variation in Total fossil CO₂ emissions. A relatively small number of large emitters occupy the upper end of the emissions scale, while many country/entity observations have considerably lower Total emissions.

The map uses log(1 + Total) for the colour scale because the raw Total-emissions distribution is strongly right-skewed. This transformation improves visual differentiation among lower- and medium-emitting geographic entities without changing the original emissions values.

The geographic pattern reinforces the earlier finding that country/entity emissions differ substantially in scale. These differences will need to be considered when evaluating a cross-country forecasting model.

The map includes ISO-coded country/entity observations and should not be interpreted as containing only sovereign countries. Territories and other non-sovereign geographic entities may still be present and will be addressed when the final modelling population is defined.

1.17 Data Understanding Summary and Modelling Implications¶

The initial data-understanding and exploratory analysis identified several characteristics that will influence the forecasting methodology.

  1. The dataset contains 63,104 observations covering 232 country/entity series from 1750 to 2021.

  2. The panel is structurally balanced by year, but variable completeness differs substantially. Total emissions are nearly complete, while source-specific variables and Per Capita contain considerably more missing values, particularly in earlier historical periods.

  3. Zero Total-emissions observations are concentrated heavily in the earlier historical period, while modern periods contain far fewer zero observations. This suggests that the full 1750–2021 period may not be equally suitable for predictive modelling.

  4. Eight historical, aggregate, regional, or special-purpose entities were identified for separate review. Additional ISO-coded territories may also remain, so the final modelling population requires a clearly defined inclusion rule.

  5. Total emissions are strongly correlated with Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, Flaring, and Other emissions. Verification using complete observations showed that the source components reproduce Total emissions within numerical rounding, confirming that same-year source values must not be used to predict same-year Total.

  6. Emissions trajectories vary substantially across countries/entities, demonstrating cross-country heterogeneity in both emissions scale and temporal behaviour.

  7. The 2021 Total-emissions distribution is extremely right-skewed. A log(1 + Total) transformation reduced skewness substantially, suggesting that transformed representations may be useful for some modelling approaches.

  8. Total and Per Capita emissions show only a weak positive relationship in 2021, indicating that they capture different aspects of national emissions behaviour.

  9. Geographic and ranking analyses show that a small number of very large emitters account for much higher Total emissions than most other country/entity observations.

These findings support a forecasting design based on historical or lagged emissions information, time-ordered validation, careful treatment of country/entity scope, and evaluation methods that account for large differences in emissions scale.

1.18 Formal Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Profiling¶

Following the initial data-understanding assessment, this section presents a more structured exploratory data analysis (EDA) and data-profiling review of the fossil CO₂ emissions dataset.

The purpose of this analysis is to examine data quality, variable distributions, missingness, zero values, extreme observations, temporal patterns, and relationships among variables before predictive modelling.

Particular attention is given to characteristics that may influence the forecasting methodology, including historically structured missingness, highly skewed emissions distributions, differences in emissions scale across countries/entities, and relationships among the emissions-source variables.

The findings from this section are used to support and justify subsequent data-preparation and modelling decisions.

1.18.1 Missing-Data Profile¶

Missing values are examined across all variables to determine which fields have incomplete observations and whether missingness may affect their suitability for modelling.

Because the dataset covers the period from 1750 to 2021, missing values are not assumed to occur randomly. The initial analysis indicated that source-specific emissions variables contain substantially more missing historical observations than Total emissions. Therefore, missingness is first quantified by variable and is later examined across time before any removal or treatment decisions are made.

Missing-Data Findings¶

Missingness varies substantially across the dataset.

The Country and Year variables are complete, while Total fossil CO₂ emissions are also nearly complete, with only approximately 0.32% missing observations.

In contrast, the source-specific emissions variables contain substantially more missing observations when the entire 1750–2021 period is considered. Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, and Flaring each have approximately 65–67% missing values, while Per Capita emissions have approximately 70% missing values. The Other emissions category is the least complete variable, with approximately 97% missing observations.

These results do not by themselves imply poor overall data quality because the dataset covers more than 270 years of historical observations. Subsequent temporal profiling showed that much of the missingness is concentrated in earlier historical periods and that completeness improves substantially in more recent decades.

For this reason, missing observations were not immediately removed or imputed. Instead, completeness was evaluated across candidate historical periods before selecting the final modelling window.

1.18.2 Numerical Distribution and Skewness Analysis¶

The distributions of the numerical emissions variables are examined to identify skewness, concentration near zero, and extreme observations.

Particular attention is given to Total fossil CO₂ emissions because it is the main forecasting target. Country/entity emissions vary substantially in scale, so the raw distribution is expected to be highly right-skewed.

Both the original scale and a logarithmic transformation are examined. The logarithmic transformation is used only for visualization and interpretation; it does not alter the original emissions values in the dataset.

Total-Emissions Distribution Findings¶

The raw distribution of Total fossil CO₂ emissions is strongly right-skewed. A large proportion of observations are zero or relatively small, while a comparatively small number of country/entity-year observations contain very large emissions values.

The log-transformed distribution makes the lower and middle portions of the emissions distribution easier to examine by compressing the scale of the largest observations. The transformation is used for visualization only and does not replace the original Total emissions values.

The boxplot also identifies many observations as statistical extremes. However, these values are not automatically treated as data errors. Large-emitting countries and aggregate entities can legitimately have emissions levels far above the majority of observations.

Therefore, extreme values are retained unless there is specific evidence of a data-quality problem. Their influence is considered later during modelling and forecast-error analysis.

1.18.3 Source-Specific Emissions Distributions¶

The distributions of the major fossil CO₂ source variables are examined to understand how emissions differ across Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, and Flaring.

These variables are important because they represent the principal source-specific emissions categories used later in the forecasting analysis. Their distributions are examined for skewness, zero concentration, and extreme observations.

Source-Specific Distribution Findings¶

The source-specific fossil CO₂ emissions variables are strongly right-skewed.

Coal and Oil contain the largest emissions values among the source categories, while Gas, Cement, and Flaring are more heavily concentrated near zero. The median values are substantially smaller than the corresponding means and maximum values, indicating that a relatively small number of high-emission observations strongly influence the distributions.

Gas and Flaring contain particularly large concentrations of zero-valued observations, while Coal, Oil, and Cement also show substantial differences between typical and extreme emissions levels.

The log-transformed histograms make the distributions more visible but confirm that substantial skewness remains across all source-specific variables.

These patterns indicate considerable heterogeneity across countries/entities and historical periods. Extreme values are retained because they may represent legitimate high-emission observations rather than data-quality errors.

1.18.4 Source-Specific Extreme-Value Assessment¶

Boxplots are used to examine the spread and statistical extreme values of the major source-specific emissions variables.

Because the emissions variables are strongly right-skewed, log(1 + x) transformed values are used for visualization. This makes the central distributions easier to inspect while preserving zero-valued observations.

Boxplot-defined outliers are treated as statistical extremes rather than automatically as data errors, because substantial differences in emissions scale are expected across countries/entities.

Source-Specific Extreme-Value Findings¶

The log-transformed boxplots show substantial differences in the distributions of the source-specific emissions variables.

Coal and Oil exhibit the widest central distributions and higher median emissions, while Gas, Cement, and especially Flaring are much more heavily concentrated near zero.

All five variables contain numerous statistical extreme values above their upper boxplot whiskers. These values are not automatically treated as data errors because large differences in emissions levels are expected across countries/entities and historical periods.

The results confirm that the source-specific emissions variables are highly heterogeneous and strongly skewed even after logarithmic transformation. This heterogeneity is retained for modelling rather than removed through automatic outlier filtering.

1.18.5 Zero-Value and Temporal Analysis¶

Zero-valued Total emissions observations are examined across different historical periods.

A zero value is treated differently from a missing value. Missing values indicate unavailable information, while zero values represent recorded observations with no reported Total emissions.

Because the dataset extends back to 1750, the proportion of zero observations is examined by historical starting period to determine whether zero concentration changes substantially over time.

In [84]:
zero_period_results = []

for start_year in [
    1750,
    1800,
    1850,
    1900,
    1950,
    1960,
    1980,
    1990,
    2000
]:

    subset = df[
        df["Year"] >= start_year
    ]

    valid_total = (
        subset["Total"]
        .dropna()
    )

    zero_count = (
        valid_total == 0
    ).sum()

    total_valid = len(
        valid_total
    )

    zero_percent = (
        zero_count
        / total_valid
        * 100
    )

    zero_period_results.append({
        "Start_Year": start_year,
        "Valid_Total_Observations": total_valid,
        "Zero_Observations": zero_count,
        "Zero_Percent": zero_percent
    })

zero_period_profile = pd.DataFrame(
    zero_period_results
)

zero_period_profile.round(2)

Zero-Value Temporal Findings¶

The proportion of zero-valued Total emissions observations declines substantially in more recent historical periods.

Across the complete 1750–2021 dataset, approximately 65.51% of valid Total observations are zero. This decreases to approximately 32.76% when the analysis begins in 1900, 10.23% from 1950 onward, and 8.30% from 1960 onward. From 2000 onward, only approximately 4.78% of valid Total observations are zero.

Zero values are not treated as missing observations or automatically removed. They represent recorded emissions values and may be legitimate. However, the strong concentration of zeros in the earlier historical period demonstrates that the statistical structure of the full 1750–2021 dataset differs substantially from that of more recent decades.

This temporal pattern is therefore considered together with variable completeness when selecting a suitable modelling period.

1.18.6 Modelling-Period Suitability Assessment¶

A suitable modelling period should provide sufficient historical coverage while also maintaining good predictor completeness and avoiding a dataset dominated by the very different zero-value structure of the earliest historical observations.

Candidate starting years are therefore compared using two profiling measures:

  • the percentage of rows with complete values across the core modelling variables; and
  • the percentage of valid Total emissions observations equal to zero.

This comparison is used to support the selection of the forecasting period rather than choosing a starting year arbitrarily.

1.18.7 Correlation and Bivariate Analysis¶

Bivariate analysis is used to examine relationships among the core numerical emissions variables.

Because the forecasting analysis uses the period from 1960 onward, the correlation assessment is performed on this same historical period. This provides a relationship profile that is more representative of the data used for modelling.

Correlation measures the strength and direction of linear association between variables. High correlation does not imply causation, and strong relationships are expected between Total emissions and source-specific emissions variables because the source categories contribute to Total emissions.

Correlation Findings¶

The correlation analysis identifies strong positive relationships among the absolute emissions variables.

Total emissions are strongly correlated with Coal (0.98), Oil (0.98), Gas (0.97), Cement (0.93), and Flaring (0.92). Strong positive relationships are also observed among many of the source-specific emissions variables themselves.

These relationships are expected because the source-specific categories contribute to overall fossil CO₂ emissions and because large-emitting countries/entities often have relatively high emissions across several source categories.

The strong correlations indicate substantial overlap in the information contained by the absolute emissions predictors. This finding is important for later regression modelling because highly correlated predictors can lead to multicollinearity and unstable individual coefficient estimates.

Per Capita emissions show very weak raw linear correlations with the absolute emissions variables. This indicates that per-capita emissions capture a different aspect of emissions intensity than absolute national/entity emissions scale.

Correlation is interpreted as statistical association rather than evidence of causation. The later modelling analysis therefore uses additional diagnostics, including Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), to assess the effect of predictor overlap.

1.18.8 Total versus Per Capita Emissions¶

A scatter plot is used to examine the relationship between absolute Total fossil CO₂ emissions and Per Capita emissions.

These variables represent different dimensions of emissions: Total measures the absolute emissions scale of a country/entity, while Per Capita measures emissions relative to population.

Because Total emissions are strongly right-skewed, a logarithmic transformation is used on the Total axis to improve visualization.

In [91]:

    ["Country", "Year", "Total", "Per Capita"]
].dropna().copy()

total_percapita["Log_Total"] = np.log1p(
    total_percapita["Total"]
)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

    total_percapita["Log_Total"],
    total_percapita["Per Capita"],
    alpha=0.4,
    s=20
)

plt.ylabel("Per Capita Fossil CO₂ Emissions (tCO₂/person)")

)

plt.grid(

    alpha=0.3
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Total versus Per Capita Findings¶

The scatter plot shows substantial variation in Per Capita emissions across countries/entities with similar levels of absolute Total emissions.

Several observations with relatively modest Total emissions have very high Per Capita emissions, while many of the largest absolute emitters have much more moderate Per Capita values. This demonstrates that absolute emissions scale and emissions intensity per person represent different characteristics of an entity.

The correlation analysis on the original variables identified only a very weak linear association between Total and Per Capita emissions (approximately 0.03). The scatter plot is consistent with this result and shows no clear simple linear pattern.

The logarithmic transformation of Total is used only to improve visualization because absolute emissions span a very large range.

1.18.9 Total versus Coal Emissions¶

The relationship between Total fossil CO₂ emissions and Coal emissions is examined as an example of the strong associations observed among the absolute emissions variables.

The raw correlation analysis identified a very strong positive relationship between Total and Coal emissions. Because both variables are strongly right-skewed, logarithmic transformations are used for visualization.

Total versus Coal Findings¶

The scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between Coal emissions and Total fossil CO₂ emissions.

The raw correlation between Total and Coal emissions is approximately 0.98, indicating a very strong linear association on the original scale. After applying logarithmic transformations to reduce the influence of extreme values, the correlation remains strong at approximately 0.849.

The relationship is more dispersed among lower-emission observations, indicating that Total emissions can remain substantial even when Coal emissions are relatively low because other source categories such as Oil, Gas, Cement, and Flaring also contribute to Total emissions.

At higher emissions levels, Coal and Total emissions follow a much tighter positive pattern. This supports the earlier correlation analysis and also helps explain why substantial predictor overlap and multicollinearity are observed later in the regression analysis.

The relationship is interpreted as statistical association rather than evidence of causation.

1.18.10 Data Profiling Constraints and Modelling Implications¶

The exploratory data analysis identified several important characteristics and constraints that directly influence the forecasting methodology.

  1. Historically structured missingness
    Total emissions are nearly complete, while source-specific variables contain substantial missingness over the full 1750–2021 period. Missingness is concentrated more heavily in earlier historical periods, so observations were not immediately removed or imputed without first examining temporal completeness.

  2. High concentration of early zero values
    Zero-valued Total emissions are much more common in the earliest historical period. The proportion of zero observations falls from approximately 65.5% across the full dataset to approximately 8.3% from 1960 onward. Zero values are treated as valid observations rather than missing data.

  3. Choice of modelling period
    Beginning the modelling period in 1960 provides approximately 90.1% completeness across the core modelling variables while retaining more than six decades of historical information. Later start dates provide only modest improvements in completeness while substantially reducing the available training history.

  4. Strong right-skewness and extreme values
    Total and source-specific emissions variables are strongly right-skewed, with many low observations and a relatively small number of very large values. Extreme observations are retained because they may represent legitimate high-emission countries/entities rather than data errors.

  5. Large differences in emissions scale
    Absolute emissions vary substantially across countries/entities. Large emitters can therefore have a disproportionate influence on aggregate error measures such as MAE and RMSE. This effect is considered during later model evaluation and residual analysis.

  6. Strong relationships among absolute emissions variables
    Total, Coal, Oil, Gas, Cement, and Flaring show very strong positive correlations. This indicates substantial overlap in the information provided by the predictors and motivates later multicollinearity assessment using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF).

  7. Per Capita measures a different emissions dimension
    Per Capita emissions show very weak raw linear relationships with the absolute emissions variables. This suggests that emissions per person capture a different aspect of emissions intensity than absolute country/entity emissions scale.

  8. Target-leakage risk
    Because Total emissions are closely related to the source-specific emissions components, using same-year source variables to predict same-year Total emissions would risk providing information that is effectively part of the target itself. The forecasting design therefore uses historical lagged predictors to predict the following year's Total emissions.

Overall, the data-profiling results support the use of a temporally restricted, leakage-safe forecasting design with chronological validation.
